name: Ossuary Light

stars.name: The Bone Lantern
stars.notes: Millisecond pulsar rotating 174 times per second. Extreme magnetic field generates persistent x-ray emission. The rapid rotation suggests it was spun up by accreting material from a companion that has since been consumed or ejected.

planets.name: The Ossicle
planets.notes: Pulsar planet formed from supernova fallback material. Diamond-rich interior under extreme pressure. Surface bathed in constant x-ray flux. Contains a single anomalous object: a tetrahedral structure 400 meters on a side, embedded in the surface as if it fell from orbit and fused with the rock.

anomalies.name: The Tetrahedron
anomalies.location: Surface of The Ossicle, northern hemisphere
anomalies.notes: Perfect tetrahedron, 400 meters per edge, partially embedded in planetary surface. Material is identical to nothing in human databases. Emits a low-power electromagnetic pulse every 11.3 seconds—a rhythm that has no mathematical relationship to the pulsar's rotation. Estimated age: older than the neutron star itself, suggesting it survived the supernova that created the pulsar.

anomalies.name: The Phantom Companion
anomalies.location: 0.4 AU from the pulsar, empty space
anomalies.notes: Pulsar timing analysis reveals gravitational influence consistent with a 0.3 solar mass object at 0.4 AU. No object is visible at this location in any wavelength. Either a dark matter concentration or an object composed of material that does not interact with electromagnetic radiation.

stations.name: Lantern Watch
stations.notes: Heavily shielded research station operated by the Pulsar Timing Consortium. Primary mission is studying the Phantom Companion; the Tetrahedron is a secondary research target due to the danger of approaching The Ossicle.

faction_control.notes: The Consortium holds a research and observation claim. The extreme radiation environment discourages any other interest.

history: The pulsar was detected by radio telescope array in 2267 and catalogued as a routine millisecond pulsar. Timing anomalies suggesting the Phantom Companion were noted in 2301 but not investigated for decades.

The Pulsar Timing Consortium dispatched a shielded probe in 2389 that discovered The Ossicle and its embedded Tetrahedron. The finding that the artifact predated the supernova—and therefore survived a stellar explosion—generated intense scientific debate.

Lantern Watch was established in 2412. Research has confirmed the Tetrahedron's anomalous age and electromagnetic pulse but has been unable to approach closer than 200 km due to radiation intensity. The Phantom Companion remains unobserved despite gravitational confirmation.
description: Ossuary Light pulses 174 times per second—a dead star spinning so fast it becomes a lighthouse of x-rays and radio waves. The Bone Lantern is a millisecond pulsar, the collapsed core of a massive star that detonated billions of years ago, and its single surviving world is a tiny diamond-cored rock bathed in radiation that would sterilize a fleet in minutes. It is not a welcoming place. The eight researchers at Lantern Watch study it from a respectful distance of over three astronomical units, peering at their instruments from behind meters of radiation shielding.

Two mysteries define this system. The first is the Tetrahedron: a 400-meter geometric solid embedded in the surface of The Ossicle, made of unknown material, pulsing with its own electromagnetic rhythm. It is older than the pulsar. This means it existed when the original star was still alive, survived the supernova that destroyed everything else in the system, and settled onto the surface of the newly formed pulsar planet as if nothing had happened. No known material can survive a supernova at close range. The Tetrahedron is not made of any known material. The second mystery is the Phantom Companion—a gravitational signature at 0.4 AU with no visible source. Something massive is there. Nothing can be seen.

The Ossuary Light is a system of ghosts and relics. An artifact that should not exist pulses on a world too irradiated to visit. An invisible mass orbits where nothing should be. The pulsar itself is a tombstone for the star it used to be. Researchers at Lantern Watch accumulate data year after year, refining their measurements of things they cannot touch or see, in a system where the deepest answers are locked behind the most lethal barriers. The Bone Lantern spins on, indifferent, its x-ray beam sweeping across the dark like a searchlight in an empty prison.
